newsitem.title: GERMANY: Germany's Pro7 TV seeks July 7 share listing.
newsitem.headline: Germany's Pro7 TV seeks July 7 share listing.

text.p: Broadcasting company Pro Sieben Media AG said on Wednesday it aims to list its shares on German stock exchanges and in a private placement in New York on July 7.

The first German broadcasting group to go public, Pro Sieben aims to open bookbuilding for its shares on June 23 with the announcement of the price range for the 17.5 million preference shares that will go up for sale two weeks later.
Pro Sieben chairman Georg Kofler told Reuters that the issue should bring in at least one billion marks, which would indicate an offer price of at least 57 marks a share.
"We are seeking a healthy mix of international and domestic shareholders as well as of private and institutional investors," Kofler said. "A billion marks plus means 57 marks plus per share."
Kofler also said he expected the company to be listed in Germany's M-DAX index of 70 companies.
The Pro Sieben group had turnover of 1.675 billion marks in 1996, up 14 percent from the year before, and pre-tax profit of 170 million marks, up from 111.4 million marks.

Over 95 percent of the company's turnover comes from its two TV stations Pro7 and Kabel1, but Kofler said in the other divisions -- merchandising, multimedia and digital television -- would eventually account for up to 20 percent of sales.

He said the company's three strategic goals were to secure and expand core business, develop television-related services, and expand the portfolio to improve the company's position in television production and licensing.
"It could also be strategically important for us to acquire a third channel, a small channel," he said.
He added that he expected Kabel1 to break even next year and that all of its losses were included in the balance sheet for 1996, so that the company would not show a loss for 1997.
Kabel1 sales totalled 200 million marks last year and its loss was around 20 million marks.
Pro Sieben is planning a reorganisation of its shareholder structure that will elevate Thomas Kirch, the son of Bavarian media mogul Leo Kirch, to majority shareholder.
After the restructuring, Thomas Kirch will hold 60 percent of Pro Sieben ordinary shares and the retail group Rewe will hold the remaining 40 percent.
The company plans initially to float 17.5 million non-voting preferred shares, but expects to offer common stock to the public at a later date.

While it has been criticised for not offering voting stock to the market, the Pro Sieben points out that other companies like software group SAP AG also entered the market with non-voting preferred stock.
Lothar Lanz, Pro Sieben finance chief, said it would be extremely difficult to float two kinds of stock simultaneously.
"That would be particularly hard to explain abroad," he said.
But Kofler stressed that it the first offer would not be the last. "We think it is probable that before the year 2000 ordinary shares in Pro Sieben will be traded on the stock exchange."
He was confident that the July issue would be a success, both in Germany and with the private placement in the United States.
"I expect there will be a double-digit over-subscription," he said, adding that U.S. investors were very keen on German media stocks.

The first 7,777 members of the company's merchandising franchise, Pro Sieben Club, which currently has some 100,000 members, to sign up for the IPO will be guaranteed allotment of at least 10 Pro Sieben shares.
-- Bonn Newsroom, 49 228 26097 150
